name: Northern Tepehuan
sweep_summary: Northern Tepehuan is not in the catalog. The one sweep item (Glottolog 669887, author-less) is Kim, Michael Jinhwa 1997, WCCFL 15: 257-272, a metrical reanalysis of Bascom's data claiming tone is predictable from stress; no open copy could be located (S2/OpenAlex/Google Books rate-limited, CSLI page gone, Wayback offline). The sweep instead turned up and read two open first-hand sources by Carlos Gil Burgoin: AMP 9 (2021), which gives an explicit rule (stress never final; disyllables initial; longer words: first heavy syllable, else second syllable; L-toned initial long vowels repel stress; NON-FINALITY >> IAMBIC-RHYTHM >> STRESS-TO-WEIGHT) with acoustic backing, and the CLECM 7 (2020) critical bibliography, which documents that Bascom 1982: 272 called stress non-contrastive and freely fluctuating, that Woo 1970 does not treat stress, and that Kim 1997 works from Bascom's data. Bascom 1982 (SIL sketch, now Cloudflare-blocked/print), Bascom 1959 and Woo 1970 (paywalled DOIs) remain unread; Bascom 1982 is the high-priority acquisition. Recommended new record: weight-sensitive initial-window stress, deciding source Gil Burgoin 2021 sec. 5.

new_statements.quote: NTep stress is generally predictable from the number of syllables of the word and from syllable weight, although there are a number of relevant exceptions. [...] disyllabic words, which, as stated above, are always stress-initial. [...] (4) Stress is never final [...] (5) i. stress falls on the first heavy σ ii. otherwise it falls on the second σ [...] When the first syllable has a long vowel (a), a consonant coda (b), or a glide coda, the stress is initial, but when the word only has short vowels the stress falls on the second (d).
new_statements.citation: Gil Burgoin, Carlos. 2021. Arguments for a Privative L Tone in Northern Tepehuan. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 9 (AMP 2020). doi:10.3765/amp.v9i0.4916
new_statements.locator: sec. 5.1 'General mechanism', pp. 3-4, statements (4)-(6); exceptions in 5.2-5.3 p. 4; constraint ranking (11) p. 5
new_statements.reading: Fixed, predictable, weight-sensitive stress confined to a left-edge two-syllable window and never final: disyllables initial; longer words stress the first heavy syllable (long vowel, consonant or glide coda; long vowels occur only in sigma-1) else the second syllable; a lexically L-toned initial long vowel repels stress to sigma-2. Same 'first heavy in a two-syllable window' shape as the catalog's Southeastern Tepehuan record (Willett 1991 / Reyes Taboada 2014). Coexists with a privative lexical L tone. First-hand data (Baborigame, two speakers, 1200-word base, acoustic measurements). Supersedes the older 'stress fluctuates freely / stress predicted from tone' lines attributed to Bascom 1959/1982.

sources.citation: Gil Burgoin, Carlos. 2021. Arguments for a Privative L Tone in Northern Tepehuan. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 9 (AMP 2020). 6 pp. doi:10.3765/amp.v9i0.4916
sources.quote: NTep stress is generally predictable from the number of syllables of the word and from syllable weight, although there are a number of relevant exceptions. [...] disyllabic words, which, as stated above, are always stress-initial. [...] (4) Stress is never final [...] (5) i. stress falls on the first heavy σ ii. otherwise it falls on the second σ [...] When the first syllable has a long vowel (a), a consonant coda (b), or a glide coda, the stress is initial, but when the word only has short vowels the stress falls on the second (d).
sources.locator: sec. 5 'Stress assignment', pp. 3-4 (also fn. 2 p. 3; sec. 8 p. 5)
sources.note: First-hand (two speakers, Baborigame; 1200-entry lexical base, F0 measured on ~700 tokens). Stress is culminative and obligatory, never final. Disyllables are always initial-stressed regardless of weight or pitch. In words of 3+ syllables stress falls on the first heavy syllable (long vowel, consonant coda or glide coda), otherwise on the second syllable; exceptions where an initial long vowel carrying a lexical L tone repels stress to sigma-2 (e.g. [baː'bádɨ] 'grandfather.3s', [iː'bɨhɨj] 'breath'). Modeled as NON-FINALITY >> IAMBIC-RHYTHM >> STRESS-TO-WEIGHT plus *ALIGN(HEAD/LOW). Correlates…

sources.citation: Gil Burgoin, Carlos Ivanhoe. 2020. Un balance crítico de los estudios lingüísticos del ódami (tepehuano del norte): De Rinaldini a la contribución de los hablantes nativos. Cuadernos de Lingüística de El Colegio de México 7, e195. 38 pp. doi:10.24201/clecm.v7i0.195
sources.quote: Sobre el primero [el acento], Bascom señala que no es contrastivo y que fluctúa libremente (Bascom 1982: 272). [...] Kim (1997), en cambio, utiliza los datos de Bascom para mostrar que el tono es predecible a partir del acento y de la estructura métrica -aunque, vistos ciertos ejemplos, es dudoso-. [Translation: On the former (stress), Bascom states that it is not contrastive and fluctuates freely (Bascom 1982: 272). Kim (1997), by contrast, uses Bascom's data to show that tone is predictable from stress and metrical structure -though, given certain examples, this is doubtful.]
sources.note: Critical bibliography, not a description. Reports that Bascom (1959: 73; 1965: 18; 1982: 271) and Woo (1970) treat the language as tonal with H and L; that Bascom 1982: 272 says stress is not contrastive and fluctuates freely; that Woo 1970 does not discuss stress at all ('Tampoco habla del acento'); and that Kim 1997 derives tone from stress and metrical structure using Bascom's data. Useful as the map of the earlier literature; the actual stress rule is in Gil Burgoin 2021.

sources.note: Not read first-hand. As reported by Gil Burgoin 2020 p. 16, Bascom 1982: 272 says stress is not contrastive and 'fluctúa libremente' (fluctuates freely); as reported by Gil Burgoin 2021 p. 1, Bascom 1982: 272 'claimed... that stress is predicted from tone, although never explained how'. The standard reference sketch and the source Kim 1997 and Woo 1970 draw on; worth acquiring because a catalog record would otherwise rest on one 6-page proceedings paper.
